final_proof:
Let \(I_n\) denote the \(n\times n\) identity matrix. We first prove the finite-dimensional fact that a linear map \(T:\mathbb F^n\to\mathbb F^n\) is injective if and only if it is surjective. If \(T\) is injective, the images under \(T\) of a basis of \(\mathbb F^n\) are \(n\) linearly independent vectors, hence form a basis; thus \(T\) is surjective. Conversely, if \(T\) is surjective, choose \(v_1,\ldots,v_n\) such that \(T(v_i)=e_i\), where \(e_1,\ldots,e_n\) is a basis. The vectors \(v_i\) are linearly independent, because applying \(T\) to a relation among them gives the corresponding relation among the \(e_i\); hence the \(v_i\) form a basis. If \(T(x)=0\), express \(x=\sum_i c_i v_i\). Applying \(T\) gives \(0=\sum_i c_i e_i\), so every \(c_i=0\) and therefore \(x=0\). Thus \(T\) is injective.

Now suppose that \(B\) is a left inverse of \(A\), so \(BA=I_n\). Regard the matrices as linear maps on \(\mathbb F^n\). If \(Ax=0\), then
\[
x=I_nx=BAx=0,
\]
so \(A\) is injective. By the fact just proved, \(A\) is surjective. Hence, for arbitrary \(y\in\mathbb F^n\), there exists \(x\in\mathbb F^n\) with \(y=Ax\). Associativity and \(BA=I_n\) then give
\[
(AB)y=AB(Ax)=A(BA)x=A I_nx=Ax=y.
\]
Thus \(AB\) fixes every vector in \(\mathbb F^n\), so \(AB=I_n\). Therefore \(B\) is also a right inverse of \(A\).

The symmetric assertion is proved in the same way. Suppose that \(B\) is a right inverse of \(A\), so \(AB=I_n\). If \(Bx=0\), then
\[
x=I_nx=ABx=0,
\]
so \(B\) is injective and hence surjective. For arbitrary \(y\in\mathbb F^n\), choose \(x\) with \(y=Bx\). Then
\[
(BA)y=BA(Bx)=B(AB)x=B I_nx=Bx=y.
\]
Consequently \(BA=I_n\), and \(B\) is also a left inverse of \(A\).

Hence a left or right inverse of a square matrix over a field is necessarily a two-sided inverse. The problem's last sentence literally repeats “right inverse”; read literally it is immediate, while the nontrivial symmetric conclusion proved above is evidently the intended one.
